entities.name: Alcidas
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alcidas, a Spartan navarch, held a critical, if ultimately unsuccessful, command during the early stages of the Peloponnesian War, specifically from 428 to 427 BCE. Tasked with supporting the Mytilenean Revolt against Athens, his leadership in the Aegean Sea exposed significant deficiencies in Spartan naval strategy and execution. His actions directly influenced the trajectory of the war's initial phase, underscoring Athens' formidable maritime power and compelling Sparta to later re-evaluate its approach to naval warfare.

Alcidas's most notable engagement began in 428 BCE when he led a Peloponnesian fleet of 42 ships to relieve Mytilene, which was under Athenian siege. His cautious and indecisive approach, however, proved disastrous. Instead of making a swift dash to Mytilene, Alcidas lingered, allowing the Athenian commander Paches to complete the circumvallation of the city. Upon learning of Mytilene's fall in 427 BCE, Alcidas's fleet, rather than engaging the Athenians, retreated, committing atrocities against Greek merchant vessels and coastal towns. His subsequent flight across the Aegean, pursued by Paches, culminated in his return to the Peloponnese without having achieved any strategic objective, only to later participate in the indecisive Battle of Corcyra in 427 BCE.

The strategic failures under Alcidas's command had profound consequences, reinforcing Athenian naval supremacy in the Aegean for years to come and highlighting Sparta's initial inability to project power effectively at sea. This episode served as a stark lesson for the Peloponnesian League, contributing to a longer-term reassessment of Spartan naval doctrine and logistics. The experience ultimately spurred later Spartan commanders, such as Lysander, to develop more sophisticated and aggressive naval strategies, which would eventually challenge and overcome Athens' maritime hegemony.
